analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $4.55 an hour in steps and sets up annual reviews for future increases.
analysis.headline: The Senate Labor Committee approved the wage increase without amendment, but the full Senate never voted on it — it set the bill aside by unanimous consent on January 24, 1990, and the 101st Congress ended without a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Senator Kennedy's bill would have raised the federal minimum wage from $3.35 to $4.55 an hour over three years, with a new review board recommending annual adjustments afterward. To soften the blow for employers, it paired the increase with a bigger tip credit, a below-minimum training wage for new workers, and a higher small-business exemption. It also extended wage-and-hour protections to House employees and added civil penalties for repeat violators. The Senate labor committee approved it, but the full Senate set it aside by unanimous consent and it never came to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the minimum wage — concentrated in restaurants, retail, and services — would get a 36% raise over three years, reaching $4.55 in 1992. Workers in Puerto Rico would get scheduled phase-ins to the full federal minimum over four to six years. House of Representatives and Architect of the Capitol employees would gain wage, overtime, and child-labor protections they previously lacked (Senate employees would get a nonbinding statement of support). Workers without a high school diploma could take up to 10 paid-free overtime hours a week for remedial education. The public would gain a standing review board recommending wage adjustments each year.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Minimum-wage workers and tipped service workers

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $3.35 to $3.85 in 1990, $4.25 in 1991, and $4.55 in 1992 — roughly a 36% increase over three years, restoring part of the value the wage had lost to inflation since its last increase in 1981.

Creates a five-member Minimum Wage Review Board that would review wage and price data every year and recommend to Congress how the minimum wage should be adjusted, replacing the pattern of letting the wage stagnate for years.

Extends the Fair Labor Standards Act's wage, overtime, and child labor protections to employees of the House of Representatives and the Architect of the Capitol, and states the Senate's sense that its own employees should get the same protections.
Adds civil penalties for repeated or willful violations of the wage and hour rules, giving the Labor Department a stronger enforcement tool against employers who break the law more than once.

Puts Puerto Rico workers on a fixed schedule to reach the full federal minimum wage — by 1993 for industries averaging $4.00-$4.64 an hour, 1994 for lower-wage industries, and 1995 for low-wage government employees covered since 1985.
Lets employers skip overtime pay for up to 10 hours a week when a worker without a high school diploma is receiving basic remedial education, encouraging employers to let workers study on the clock.

analysis.who_pays: Employers of low-wage labor — restaurants, retail stores, and small businesses — would bear the higher payroll, softened by the bill's offsets: the tip credit rises so employers can count half the minimum wage from tips, new workers could be paid a subminimum training wage for their first 60 days, and businesses with under $500,000 in annual sales are dropped from full coverage (though businesses already covered in 1988 must keep paying at least $3.35). Consumers could see some of the cost passed through in prices, and studies of the wage's effects would be federally funded.
analysis.who_pays_short: Restaurants, retailers, and small low-wage employers

drawbacks.text: The tip credit rises from 40% to 50% of the minimum wage, meaning employers could count tips toward half the wage — so tipped workers' guaranteed cash pay would rise well below the headline minimum, from $2.01 to only about $2.27 an hour in 1992.

New workers could legally be paid a subminimum training wage of $3.35 (later 85% of the minimum) for their first cumulative 60 days of employment — $1.20 less than the 1992 minimum — and the worker, not the employer, bears responsibility for proving prior employment history that limits eligibility.
The small-business exemption threshold rises from $362,500 to $500,000 in annual sales, removing some businesses and their workers from minimum wage, overtime, and child labor coverage entirely.
The review board can only recommend adjustments — Congress would still have to act each time, so unlike true indexing, future increases could stall just as past ones did.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: a 36% wage increase for the lowest-paid workers plus annual review to prevent another decade of erosion. But the bill pays for much of the increase with offsets aimed at the same low-wage workforce — half the minimum would come from tips, new workers could be hired below the minimum for two months, and some small-firm workers would lose coverage altogether. An honest supporter would acknowledge that tipped workers, recent hires, and employees of newly exempt small businesses gain far less than the headline number suggests, while employers get meaningful cost relief in exchange for accepting the raise.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate's labor committee approved the bill and put it on the chamber's calendar, but on January 24, 1990 the Senate indefinitely postponed it by unanimous consent — meaning no senator even objected to shelving it — and it never came up for a floor vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Kennedy introduced the bill on June 14, 1989, and it was referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources, which he led the bill through.

On August 2, 1989, the committee ordered the bill reported favorably without amendment, and on August 30 it was formally reported with a written report to which minority views were filed — signaling committee Republicans' disagreement.
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders on August 30, 1989, putting it in line for a floor vote.

It sat on the calendar for nearly five months; on January 24, 1990, the Senate indefinitely postponed it by unanimous consent, removing it from the calendar, and no vote was ever held before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

The quiet death came months after President George H.W. Bush and congressional Republicans had pushed back against Senate Democratic minimum wage proposals larger than $4.25, setting the terms of the fight over wage levels that year.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of minimum-wage workers — restaurants, retailers, and small businesses — were spared this bill's $4.55 wage, subminimum-training-wage rollback limits, and annual review board. Low-wage workers got nothing from this bill, though a smaller increase (to $4.25) did become law later in 1989 through separate legislation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Low-wage employers; workers got a smaller raise elsewhere

for.name: Edward M. Kennedy
for.role: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; bill's sponsor and committee floor manager
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and reported it out of the Labor and Human Resources Committee favorably and without amendment.

for.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
for.what_they_did: Ordered the bill reported favorably without amendment on August 2, 1989, and placed it on the Senate calendar.

against.name: The Senate
against.what_they_did: Indefinitely postponed the bill by unanimous consent on January 24, 1990, removing it from the calendar without any roll-call vote and never bringing it to the floor.

against.name: Committee Republicans
against.role: Minority members, Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Filed minority views to the committee report opposing the bill as reported.

against.name: President George H.W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed Democratic minimum wage proposals above $4.25 an hour and pushed for a smaller increase with a lower youth wage, shaping the terms of the debate.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call votes were ever held on the bill; the Democratic-led committee reported it favorably but with minority views filed by Republicans, consistent with the party split over minimum wage levels that dominated the issue that Congress.

industries.note: The industry's low-wage, tip-heavy workforce makes it the bill's largest cost center, but the tip credit rising to 50% lets employers count tips toward half the minimum, cutting the net increase. The industry's interest in minimizing the raise runs against workers' interest in the full wage.

These employers would pay the full higher minimum for their largely minimum-wage workforces, with the training wage as their main offset. Lower labor costs come directly at the expense of the workers' paychecks.

industries.industry: Small businesses under $500,000 in annual sales
industries.note: The bill raises the exemption threshold from $362,500 to $500,000, freeing smaller firms from wage, overtime, and child labor rules — though firms already covered in 1988 must keep paying at least $3.35. The gain for these firms comes by removing their workers from federal protections.

The bill directs the Labor Department to treat computer systems analysts and software engineers as exempt professionals from overtime rules, even when paid hourly, if they earn at least 6.5 times the minimum wage. This is an employer-friendly clarification for already well-paid workers.

industries.industry: Employers in Puerto Rico and the island territories
industries.note: Puerto Rico employers get slower, staggered phase-ins to the full minimum wage — up to six years for low-wage government employers — while Virgin Islands special industry committees are ended and American Samoa's arrangement continues. Puerto Rico workers win guaranteed convergence with the federal minimum on a set schedule.
